paragraphs: ALTo addresses how multimodal language models represent segmentation masks: the regions marking which image pixels belong to an object. Fixed token representations impose a rigid budget even though shapes differ in complexity. The paper proposes letting the representation length adapt, making token allocation part of the mask generation process itself.

The tokenizer combines a predictor for token length, a regularization term that influences length, and a differentiable strategy for grouping tokens into chunks. These components support learning an adaptive representation. The authors then integrate the tokenizer into a multimodal language model, producing ALToLLM for generating masks autoregressively, one token after another.

ALToLLM also uses group relative policy optimization to incorporate preferences about the balance between mask quality and efficiency. Experiments report state-of-the-art segmentation performance with adaptive token costs on popular benchmarks. The contribution is therefore both a flexible mask representation and a way to train its quality–efficiency trade-off, rather than treating representation length as a fixed design choice.
neurips-2025-alto-adaptive-length-tokeni.tldr: ALTo adapts the token length used to generate segmentation masks and learns preferences over mask quality and efficiency.

paragraphs: Multiview vision models must relate images taken by different cameras to a shared three-dimensional scene. This paper examines how transformers should receive camera information so that their visual tokens carry useful geometric context. It compares camera encodings attached to individual tokens with relative encodings introduced into the attention mechanism between tokens.

The proposed Projective Positional Encoding, or PRoPE, represents relationships between complete camera frustums. It includes both camera intrinsics and extrinsics, accounting for the camera’s imaging geometry as well as its placement. This gives relative conditioning access to more complete camera information than a representation based on relative camera pose alone.

Experiments first show improvements from relative conditioning in feedforward novel view synthesis, with further gains from PRoPE. Benefits appear with shared or varying intrinsics, combined conditioning methods, and unfamiliar input sequence lengths and camera intrinsics. Results also extend to stereo depth estimation, discriminative spatial cognition, and larger models, supporting the usefulness of this representation across the tested settings.
neurips-2025-cameras-as-relative-positio.tldr: PRoPE encodes complete relative camera geometry in transformer attention, improving several tested multiview vision tasks.

paragraphs: Repository-level software tasks require understanding how functions and files fit together, beyond generating a single function in isolation. This paper investigates whether open-source language models can handle such tasks without an agent-based approach. Its central idea is to expose both the meaning of code and the structural dependencies connecting a repository.

Code Graph Models incorporate a repository’s graph structure directly into the language model’s attention mechanism. A specialized adapter translates attributes of graph nodes into the model’s input space. The resulting model is paired with an agentless graph retrieval-augmented generation framework, connecting graph-informed representation with retrieval of repository information for the task.

Using Qwen2.5-72B, the combined system achieves a 43.00% resolution rate on SWE-bench Lite. The abstract reports first place among open-weight models, second among methods with open-source systems, and eighth overall in its comparison. These results support the feasibility of repository-level problem solving with an open model and explicit code structure, while directly evaluating the combined model-and-retrieval approach.
neurips-2025-code-graph-model-cgm-a-grap.tldr: CGM integrates repository graphs into a language model and achieves 43.00% resolution on SWE-bench Lite with agentless graph retrieval.

paragraphs: Some forecasts change the outcomes they predict, making correctness itself difficult to define. The paper studies this performative setting and shows that conditioning on covariates that separate the forecast from the outcome makes the target distribution invariant to the forecast. Under that condition, the forecasting problem has a well-defined target.

Having a well-defined target does not automatically make conventional evaluation incentives work. The authors prove an impossibility result showing that classical proper scoring rules can fail to elicit correct forecasts even after this conditioning. This distinguishes two problems: establishing what the forecast should predict and rewarding a forecaster for reporting it correctly.

The paper identifies two solutions. In decision-theoretic settings, correct, incentive-compatible elicitation is possible when forecasts are separating. Another solution scores forecasts using unbiased estimates of divergence from the induced target distribution. Applied to parameter estimation, the analysis also yields performatively stable estimation of performatively correct parameters. These results provide conditional routes to reliable forecasting while exposing a fundamental failure of classical scoring.
neurips-2025-conditional-forecasts-and-p.tldr: The paper establishes conditions for well-defined performative forecasts and identifies scoring approaches that can elicit correct predictions.

paragraphs: The paper studies prediction sets when labeled training data and unlabeled deployment data come from domains with different covariate distributions. Its goal is valid marginal coverage in the target domain: the sets should include the correct answer at the desired overall frequency. This matters when uncertainty estimates must transfer across domains.

Many existing approaches require estimating a likelihood ratio between source and target distributions, which can become difficult for high-dimensional inputs. The proposed likelihood ratio regularized quantile regression method, LR-QR, instead constructs a threshold function using pinball loss and a new regularization choice. It avoids directly estimating that unknown ratio as a separate function.

The authors prove target-domain coverage at the desired level up to a small, controllable error, using stability bounds from learning theory. Experiments report improvements over existing methods on regression with Communities and Crime data, image classification from WILDS, and MMLU question answering. Together, the findings connect a qualified coverage guarantee with empirical performance across several kinds of prediction task.
neurips-2025-conformal-inference-under-h.tldr: LR-QR constructs prediction sets under covariate shift without directly estimating likelihood ratios, with target coverage guaranteed up to controllable error.

paragraphs: DeepDiver addresses information seeking on the live web, where answering a question can require repeated searches and reconsideration of the evidence. The paper introduces WebPuzzle, containing 24,000 training samples and 275 test samples across wiki and open-domain queries. This provides a setting for studying search behavior beyond well-structured wiki sources.

Using 7,000 WebPuzzle instances, the authors train models through an initial supervised fine-tuning stage followed by reinforcement learning. The resulting behavior, called Search Intensity Scaling, increases search frequency and depth instead of prematurely settling on an answer with insufficient evidence. The focus is on learning how much information gathering a response requires.

With this framework, Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct and Pangu-7B-Reasoner reach performance comparable to the 671-billion-parameter DeepSeek-R1 on the reported real-web tasks. The learned seeking policy also transfers from closed-ended questions to open-ended generation, including long-form writing. These findings support adaptive search as a useful learned capability in the evaluated settings, alongside the contribution of a live-internet benchmark.
neurips-2025-deepdiver-adaptive-web-sear.tldr: DeepDiver uses reinforcement learning to teach language models to increase web-search effort when gathering evidence.

paragraphs: Federated learning must sometimes address fairness both across the entire collection of clients and within each individual client. Those objectives need to be handled together, especially for multiclass decisions. FedFACT targets this problem while allowing a chosen balance between predictive accuracy and disparities across sensitive groups, rather than treating fairness as one fixed operating point.

The framework characterizes Bayes-optimal classifiers subject to global and local fairness constraints. These are the classifiers with the best achievable predictive performance under the specified constraints. The authors use those characterizations to formulate fairness during training as personalized cost-sensitive learning, and adjustment after training as a bilevel optimization problem.

The theory supplies convergence and generalization guarantees for approaching near-optimal accuracy at given fairness levels. Experiments across multiple datasets and different degrees of client data heterogeneity report a better accuracy–fairness balance than the baselines. The contribution connects explicit fairness targets to an optimal-classifier analysis and practical calibration methods, with empirical evidence covering both global and local disparities.
neurips-2025-fedfact-a-provable-framewor.tldr: FedFACT provides controllable global and local fairness constraints for federated learning, with theory and experiments supporting its accuracy–fairness balance.

paragraphs: Incremental sequence classification updates a prediction as more of a sequence becomes available. The paper asks how those successive predictions should relate to one another during training. Rather than considering each observed prefix independently, it identifies a temporal-consistency condition inspired by temporal-difference learning in reinforcement learning and builds a training objective around it.

The resulting loss uses that relationship between successive predictions to train an incremental classifier. A concrete example demonstrates that optimizing this objective can substantially improve data efficiency. This is a qualified demonstration of what the loss can achieve, connecting the consistency condition to learning more effectively from the available sequence data.

Experiments on several text classification benchmarks show higher predictive accuracy than competing approaches. The authors also study partial language-model solutions to grade-school math problems, where the classifier judges whether a generation is promising before it finishes. Models trained with the proposed method distinguish promising from unpromising generations better after only a few tokens, showing value for judgments made from incomplete sequences.
neurips-2025-incremental-sequence-classi.tldr: A temporal-consistency training loss improves incremental text classification and early judgments of mathematical generations in the reported experiments.

paragraphs: Point tracking follows particular locations through a video as objects and cameras move. ITTO is a benchmark suite designed to test this capability under complex real-world dynamics. Its videos combine material from existing datasets with egocentric recordings, and its human annotations are collected through multiple stages to support high-quality evaluation.

The benchmark emphasizes complicated motion, varied objects, and patterns of occlusion, where a tracked point temporarily disappears from view. The authors argue that these factors are largely absent from current benchmarks. They analyze state-of-the-art trackers along specific dimensions of motion complexity, making the evaluation useful for diagnosing where a method struggles.

The results reveal substantial difficulties, especially when trackers must identify the same point again after an occlusion. This finding separates maintaining a visible track from recovering its identity after a gap. ITTO therefore contributes both an evaluation resource and evidence of concrete failure modes, intended to guide modeling approaches that better handle the dynamics present in real-world videos.
neurips-2025-is-this-tracker-on-a-benchm.tldr: ITTO tests point tracking under complex real-world motion and exposes particular weaknesses in recovering points after occlusion.

paragraphs: Semantic correspondence finds meaningfully matching locations across different instances of an object category. This paper shows that recent supervised methods can remain tied to the sparse keypoints used for training, behaving effectively as keypoint detectors. Success on familiar annotated locations therefore does not necessarily establish an ability to match other parts of an object.

The proposed method lifts two-dimensional keypoints into a shared canonical three-dimensional space using monocular depth estimation. It constructs a continuous canonical manifold that represents object geometry, without requiring explicit three-dimensional supervision or camera annotations. This geometric representation is intended to support dense correspondences beyond the isolated locations that received training labels.

The authors also introduce SPair-U, extending SPair-71k with new keypoint annotations to evaluate this generalization. Their model significantly outperforms supervised baselines on unseen keypoints. Separately, unsupervised baselines outperform supervised counterparts in cross-dataset generalization experiments. These findings make the evaluation target central: matching known keypoints, matching unseen locations, and transferring between datasets test different aspects of correspondence learning.
neurips-2025-jamais-vu-exposing-the-gene.tldr: A canonical 3D representation improves correspondence on unseen keypoints, while new evaluations expose generalization weaknesses in supervised methods.

paragraphs: Graphons provide a mathematical framework for representing connection patterns in large networks, but estimating them remains difficult. This paper proposes an additive representation with low rank. Its distinctive aim is to obtain low-rank structure in both the graphon and the connection probability matrix, two related objects that existing approaches rarely make low rank together.

The method also resolves identification issues, addressing ambiguity in the representation being estimated. On that basis, the authors construct an efficient sequential algorithm using counts of subgraphs and interpolation. The approach connects observable network patterns to estimation of the underlying connection structure through a representation designed to remain compact at both levels.

The authors establish consistency, providing theoretical support for the estimator’s convergence as information increases within the analyzed setting. Simulations and data analysis also show strong estimation accuracy and computational efficiency. The contribution combines a structural modeling choice, an estimation procedure, and theoretical justification: low rank serves as a shared organizing principle for the network’s probability matrix and its graphon.
neurips-2025-low-rank-graphon-learning-f.tldr: The paper jointly models graphons and connection probability matrices with low rank, enabling efficient estimation with a consistency guarantee.

paragraphs: This paper asks whether text datasets retain recognizable signatures of how they were curated, even when they originate from the same web crawl. It examines several open-source language-model pretraining datasets derived from CommonCrawl. The central experiment trains neural networks to identify which dataset supplied a single text sequence, treating dataset identity as a classification target.

The classifiers perform surprisingly well and significantly better than humans, despite similarities in the datasets’ curation processes. The authors locate these fingerprints in formatting, vocabulary, and content distributions. Their findings indicate that small filtering and processing differences leave systematic traces, and that such traces can negatively affect generalization between datasets.

The study then tests whether those signatures survive model training. A classifier trained on original dataset text can accurately classify sequences generated by models trained on those datasets. This suggests that generated outputs can reveal aspects of training-data characteristics. The authors identify possible applications to understanding otherwise undisclosed pretraining mixture proportions and fine-tuning sources, rather than establishing universal recovery of training data.
neurips-2025-measuring-fingerprints-of-w.tldr: Web-text curation leaves recognizable dataset fingerprints that can persist in the outputs of language models trained on that text.

paragraphs: Tabular foundation models can learn from synthetic datasets and then make predictions on real tables using examples supplied in context. This makes the distributions used to generate synthetic training data an important design choice. The paper investigates which properties of those distributions help a pretrained model generalize, addressing a gap in guidance for synthetic prior design.

The authors use that investigation to build Mitra, trained on a curated mixture of synthetic priors. The selection considers diversity, distinctiveness, and performance on real-world tabular data. Thus, the approach combines different data-generating assumptions while explicitly examining their usefulness, making the composition of synthetic training experience central to the model’s design.

Mitra consistently outperforms TabPFNv2 and TabICL across the reported classification and regression benchmarks, with better sample efficiency. The findings support careful prior selection as a practical route to stronger tabular foundation models. They also connect the study’s investigation of prior properties to a concrete model whose reported gains cover both categorical and numerical prediction tasks.
neurips-2025-mitra-mixed-synthetic-prior.tldr: Mitra mixes carefully selected synthetic training priors to improve tabular classification, regression, and sample efficiency on reported benchmarks.

paragraphs: In a networked experiment, treating one person can affect another person’s outcome. This interference complicates causal estimation and becomes especially consequential when decisions are made sequentially. Random assignment may help estimate effects, but repeatedly choosing inferior options also accumulates regret. The paper studies how to balance learning accurate effects with making better decisions during the experiment.

Its framework represents available choices using exposure mapping, which accounts for treatment context within the network. This extends the arm space beyond a representation that treats an individual’s assignment in isolation. The resulting formulation gives online experimental design a way to express treatment effects that depend on exposure to other participants’ assignments.

The authors establish a Pareto-optimal trade-off between estimation accuracy and regret, accounting for both the experiment’s time span and arm space. They report that this trade-off improves on baseline models even without network interference. An algorithmic implementation accompanies the analysis, along with discussion of extensions across learning settings and network topologies. The contribution explicitly links causal measurement quality to the cost of exploratory decisions.
neurips-2025-online-experimental-design-.tldr: The paper develops an interference-aware online experiment framework with a Pareto-optimal trade-off between causal estimation accuracy and regret.

paragraphs: Open-vocabulary segmentation aims to identify image regions belonging to classes absent from training. This paper examines what happens when the training collection itself keeps growing through newly collected datasets. The authors first evaluate retraining, fine-tuning, and continual learning in this setting and find limitations in each, motivating a method designed for sequential data acquisition.

Their method, ConOVS, uses a mixture of expert decoders. For each input, it estimates the probability that the sample belongs to the distribution associated with each incremental dataset. Those probabilities determine how the experts are combined, making the decoding process responsive to which accumulated data distributions best match the current image.

Experiments show consistent improvements over existing methods across pretraining, incremental, and zero-shot test datasets. This evaluation checks performance on earlier data, newly introduced data, and classes tested without corresponding training examples. The reported results support ConOVS as a way to expand recognition capabilities as datasets arrive over time, bringing continual learning into a setting usually studied with a fixed training collection.
neurips-2025-ovs-meets-continual-learnin.tldr: ConOVS combines expert decoders according to input-distribution probabilities to improve open-vocabulary segmentation as new datasets arrive.

paragraphs: Graphs can contain structural patterns that a space with one uniform global curvature represents poorly. This paper studies graph embeddings in pseudo-Riemannian manifolds, a geometric framework that generalizes hyperbolic and spherical geometries. It addresses three obstacles identified in earlier approaches: an ineffective geometric framework, shallow architectures, and insufficient guidance for choosing an appropriate manifold.

The authors introduce a diffeomorphic framework for embedding graphs and use it to construct a pseudo-Riemannian Graph Transformer. The framework gives principled definitions of linear attention, residual connections, and layer normalization within the chosen geometry. These components connect the mathematical representation space to the operations needed for a transformer architecture.

A lightweight search algorithm also selects a suitable pseudo-Riemannian manifold for an input graph, making geometry selection part of the approach. Experiments on diverse real-world graphs report consistent improvements over baselines in node classification and link prediction. The contribution therefore combines geometric representation, architecture, and space selection, with evidence that the resulting system benefits both node-level decisions and predictions about graph connections.
neurips-2025-pseudo-riemannian-graph-tra.tldr: The proposed graph transformer combines pseudo-Riemannian geometry with principled transformer operations and automatic manifold selection.

paragraphs: The paper proves that REINFORCE converges to globally optimal policies in finite-horizon Markov decision processes with any constant learning rate. The result removes the need for a small or shrinking learning rate in this convergence analysis. Its significance is theoretical: it concerns eventual optimality, including step sizes for which standard optimization arguments do not apply.

The proof begins with stochastic bandits and establishes a stronger exploration property. Online stochastic policy gradient samples every action infinitely often, extending previous results that guaranteed this for at least two actions. This shows that the method itself supplies asymptotic exploration in the analyzed setting, without an added exploration modification.

The authors also remove an assumption that mean rewards must be distinct. That matters because the earlier bandit assumption does not carry over to general Markov decision processes. Together, these advances enable the extension from bandits to finite-horizon decision problems. The findings clarify how exploration and exploitation can support convergence even with large constant updates, rather than requiring conventional small-step analysis.
neurips-2025-reinforce-converges-to-opti.tldr: REINFORCE is proved to converge to globally optimal policies in finite-horizon MDPs with any constant learning rate.

paragraphs: A binary preference label says which option someone favors, but not how strongly. ResponseRank tries to recover information about that strength from noisy signals such as response time or annotator agreement. The challenge is that these signals can reflect other systematic differences, making their raw values unreliable as direct measurements of preference intensity.

The method compares signals locally within carefully constructed strata that control for systematic variation. It uses relative differences to rank pairwise-comparison responses by inferred preference strength, then learns utility differences consistent with those rankings. This relies on locally valid comparisons and minimal assumptions, rather than requiring every signal value to provide a globally comparable strength measurement.

Experiments report better sample efficiency and robustness in synthetic preference learning, language modeling, and reinforcement-learning control. These settings use simulated response times, annotator agreement, and simulated episode returns, respectively. The paper also introduces Pearson Distance Correlation, a metric intended to separate learning utility magnitudes from merely ordering options correctly. Together, these contributions address both learning preference strength and evaluating whether it was learned.
neurips-2025-responserank-data-efficient.tldr: ResponseRank learns preference strength from locally comparable noisy signals, improving sample efficiency and robustness in the reported tasks.

paragraphs: Graph convolutional networks learn by combining information from connected nodes. The paper argues that using the graph Laplacian norm to suppress information from immediate neighbors can weaken valuable interactions. When useful relationships are sparse, this dilution may slow their discovery during training and reduce predictive performance. The work targets that particular aggregation behavior.

BoostGCN is a linear graph convolutional model that instead amplifies significant interactions with first-order neighbors. Its aim is to make important local relationships easier to capture accurately and quickly. The method keeps linear aggregation while changing the emphasis placed on useful neighbor interactions, making the treatment of local information its central design choice.

Experiments on four real-world datasets show improvements over existing state-of-the-art graph convolutional models in both performance and efficiency. The authors also describe BoostGCN as having relatively fixed parameters, supporting ease of use. These results provide empirical support for amplification in the evaluated settings, linking the proposed handling of neighbor information to both prediction quality and the efficiency of learning.
neurips-2025-revolutionizing-graph-aggre.tldr: BoostGCN amplifies significant immediate-neighbor interactions and improves performance and efficiency on four real-world datasets.

paragraphs: Dynamic Policy Gradient, or DynPG, studies tabular decision problems that continue indefinitely while discounting future rewards. Its central idea is to combine policy gradient methods with dynamic programming, explicitly using the environment’s Markov structure. The framework is designed to work with any policy gradient method while changing how the overall learning problem is organized.

DynPG adjusts the problem horizon during training and decomposes the infinite-horizon task into a sequence of contextual bandit problems. Iteratively solving those problems leads to the stationary optimal policy of the original task. This uses the structure of sequential decisions to guide optimization, rather than treating the entire infinite-horizon objective as an undifferentiated policy-learning problem.

For tabular softmax policies, the authors establish a non-asymptotic global convergence rate and analyze its dependence on important problem parameters. In particular, the dependence on effective horizon is polynomial. This contrasts with recent exponential lower-bound examples for vanilla policy gradient, showing how incorporating dynamic-programming structure changes the available convergence guarantees in the specified setting.
neurips-2025-structure-matters-dynamic-p.tldr: DynPG combines dynamic programming with policy gradients and achieves polynomial effective-horizon scaling for tabular softmax policies.

paragraphs: Optimal transport compares distributions by the cost of moving mass between them, but its classical balanced form requires equal total mass. Partial transport allows only some mass to move, offering flexibility when data contain noise, outliers, imbalance, or structural mismatches. Its computational cost remains a challenge, particularly when solving large transport problems in high-dimensional spaces.

The paper introduces Partial Tree-Sliced Wasserstein distance by extending tree-sliced transport to this partial setting. The key observation is that partial transport on a tree-metric space can be reformulated exactly as balanced transport between suitably modified measures. This lets the method use the computational advantages of transport on trees while retaining the ability to leave some mass unmatched.

The resulting framework is designed to preserve partial transport’s adaptability and robustness with more efficient computation. The reported applications include outlier removal and handling class imbalance in image-to-image translation. These results connect the mathematical reformulation to tasks where forcing all mass to participate in a match can be undesirable, giving the partial formulation a concrete computational route.
neurips-2025-tree-sliced-entropy-partial.tldr: PartialTSW makes partial transport efficient by reformulating it as balanced transport between modified measures on tree-metric spaces.

paragraphs: Influence maximization selects starting nodes to spread information through a network. When nodes have different values, a common approach assigns each a fixed gain. This paper challenges that assumption: the gain from activating a node can depend on which surrounding nodes are already active, so it can change during diffusion even when the network structure stays fixed.

There is also a causal measurement problem. A node’s gain compares outcomes under activation and non-activation, but only one of those states is observed after propagation. The proposed Causal Influence Maximization framework uses causal inference to model dynamic individual gains, addressing both this unobservable comparison and sensitivity to the changing activation environment.

The authors introduce two algorithms, G-CauIM and A-CauIM, with an acceleration technique in the latter. They establish a generalized lower bound on influence spread and analyze robustness. Experiments on synthetic and real-world datasets support the approach’s effectiveness and reliability. The contribution brings changing, causally defined benefits into seed selection instead of assuming that a node’s importance remains constant throughout diffusion.
neurips-2025-unveiling-environmental-sen.tldr: CauIM uses causal inference to model node gains that change with surrounding activations during information diffusion.

paragraphs: UiD lets users choose which image regions should appear sharp or blurred through text, box, or point prompts. The system targets depth-of-field control, where blur helps express photographic intent. It uses dual-pixel sensor data, which provide a small-baseline stereo pair from a single snapshot and support estimation of depth-dependent imaging effects.

The method learns an invertible mapping between out-of-focus and all-in-focus images, together with spatially varying defocus kernels and disparity features. These kernels describe blur that changes across the image. Switching between a kernel and its inverse supports both recovering an all-in-focus representation and applying blur again, linking restoration and refocusing within one framework.

For user control, SAM produces masks from the supplied prompts. Those masks modulate disparity features, allowing the system to re-estimate kernels for the requested reblurring effect. Experiments on common datasets and a self-collected dataset report superior flexibility and image quality. The contribution connects user-selected focus regions to a depth-aware blur process grounded in dual-pixel observations.
neurips-2025-user-instructed-disparity-a.tldr: UiD combines dual-pixel depth cues with text, box, or point prompts to control image refocusing and blur.

paragraphs: Vector databases use approximate nearest-neighbor queries to retrieve similar vectors and can be valuable targets for unauthorized copying. This paper proposes embedding hidden information for ownership authentication. Its watermarking pipeline generates identifiers, groups vectors, applies cryptographic mapping, and modifies selected vectors. The central challenge is preserving retrieval quality despite those modifications.

The authors examine the widely used HNSW index and find that its edge-selection and pruning heuristics leave some vectors with few edges or none. These vectors are queried much less frequently. Transparent Vector Priority, or TVP, takes advantage of this uneven usage by placing watermark modifications preferentially in these low-query-frequency vectors.

The approach therefore chooses embedding locations according to their expected effect on retrieval, rather than treating all vectors as equally consequential. Experiments report approximately 75% fewer missed and false queries than the most effective relevant watermarking schemes used for comparison. This supports the strategy as a way to reduce watermark-induced query disruption while retaining the ownership-authentication purpose of the watermark.
neurips-2025-vector-database-watermarkin.tldr: TVP embeds ownership watermarks in rarely queried vectors, reducing missed and false queries by approximately 75% in reported comparisons.

paragraphs: WUKONG generates textured three-dimensional transitions between source and target prompts supplied as text or images. It is a training-free framework that uses the generative prior of flow-based transformers. This addresses a difficulty in conventional morphing workflows, which depend on manual correspondence matching and deformation-trajectory estimation, requiring costly preprocessing and limiting generalization.

For geometry, the method uses continuity in the flow-based generative process and formulates morphing as an optimal transport barycenter problem. A sequential initialization strategy is designed to prevent abrupt shape distortions and preserve coherent identity through the transition. These components organize the intermediate shapes so that the transformation remains geometrically smooth.

For appearance, a similarity-guided semantic consistency mechanism selectively preserves high-frequency texture details and controls blending dynamics. This is intended to avoid oversmoothing while maintaining semantic fidelity. Quantitative and qualitative evaluations report significant improvements over state-of-the-art methods across varied geometry and texture changes. The contribution treats smooth shape evolution and faithful texture evolution as coordinated parts of the morphing problem.
neurips-2025-wukong-s-72-transformations.tldr: WUKONG uses pretrained flow models to generate smooth, richly textured 3D morphs between text or image prompts without additional training.
